claim: A moss once handed Danish police one of the oldest fingerprints ever taken.

start.title: Moss
start.description: Division of typically non-vascular land plants

end.title: Tollund Man
end.description: Iron Age bog body from Denmark

knots.passage: The main commercial significance of mosses is as the main constituent of peat (mostly the genus Sphagnum), although they are also used for decorative purposes, such as in gardens and in the florist trade. Traditional uses of mosses included as insulation and for the ability to absorb liquids up to 20 times their weight.
knots.hatnote: Moss looks humble, but one kind quietly builds whole landscapes of peat.

knots.passage: Sphagnum and the peat formed from it do not decay readily because of the phenolic compounds embedded in the moss's cell walls. In addition, bogs, like all wetlands, develop anaerobic soil conditions, which produces slower anaerobic decay rather than aerobic microbial action. Peat moss can also acidify its surroundings by taking up cations, such as calcium and magnesium, and releasing hydrogen ions.
knots.hatnote: Peat moss has a strange talent: it barely rots.

knots.passage: Anaerobic acidic sphagnum bogs have low rates of decay, and hence preserve plant fragments and pollen to allow reconstruction of past environments. They even preserve human bodies for millennia; examples of these preserved specimens are Tollund Man, Haraldskær Woman, Clonycavan Man and Lindow Man. Such bogs can also preserve human hair and clothing, one of the most noteworthy examples being Egtved Girl, Denmark. Because of the acidity of peat, however, bones are dissolved rather than preserved. These bogs have also been used to preserve food. Up to 2000-year-old containers of butter or lard have been found.
knots.hatnote: A bog that won't rot becomes a time capsule, for butter and for people.

knots.passage: On 8 May 1950, Tollund Man was discovered in the peat layer of the peat bog, 12 km (7.5 mi) west of Silkeborg, Denmark, by peat cutters Viggo and Emil Hojgaard after Viggo's wife, Grethe Hojgaard, noticed his body in a peat pit. His remains were so well preserved that the family believed they had discovered the victim of a recent murder, and the police were called.
knots.hatnote: In 1950, Danish peat cutters found someone in the bog.

knots.passage: Both feet and the right thumb were placed in formalin after the examination. Twenty-six years later, in 1976, the Danish police recorded a usable fingerprint from the preserved thumb, making it one of the oldest fingerprints obtained from human remains.
knots.hatnote: The police didn't get a murder case, but they did get a souvenir.

payoff: Peat moss barely rots, so a bog kept a man for millennia, fresh enough to fool the police, right down to his thumbprint.
